text: Last lesson established that task is a base table other tables extend. Now let's put real names on that tree. Directly extending task are three tables: incident, problem, and change_request. Each of these is a genuine table name you'll use constantly as an admin — incident.list and incident.do, from Lesson 5's direct-navigation shortcut, work precisely because incident is a real table, not just a label painted over task.

The Service Catalog's structure runs one level deeper. When someone submits a catalog request, ordering a laptop or requesting software access, ServiceNow creates a request record on sc_request, which itself extends task. That request can contain multiple requested items, each one a record on sc_req_item, which extends sc_request in turn. A single laptop order might produce one sc_request for the overall order, and one sc_req_item for the specific laptop line item.

That two-level structure is why a catalog request can carry one overall state while each item inside it tracks its own fulfillment separately. And both records, by extension, are still task records underneath it all — which is the whole point of this hierarchy: everything traces back to the same foundation, no matter how many levels of extension sit in between the leaf table and task itself.

Now you can see the technical reason Incident, Problem, and Change Management from Course 1 felt so similar to administer. The state field driving an incident's lifecycle — new, in progress, resolved, closed — is the exact same field mechanism driving a change request's lifecycle. The assignment-group routing you configure for incidents works the same way for problems. Priority, calculated from impact times urgency, is task-level logic, never written three separate times.

When you're unsure whether a behavior is specific to one table or shared platform-wide, ask whether the field exists on task itself. If it does, expect the same field, behaving the same way, on every table in this hierarchy, including custom tables an admin later builds by extending task. If it doesn't, it's specific to that one branch. Next up: how tables point at each other through reference fields.
